text:
Shipping’s proposed global carbon price has survived another bruising week at the International Maritime Organization, with a clear majority of countries continuing to back the core architecture of the Net-Zero Framework ahead of a decisive round of talks in December.

Nearly 1,200 delegates participated in last week’s ISWG-GHG 22 meeting in London, where governments attempted to bridge divisions that derailed formal adoption of the framework last year.

Thirty-eight countries speaking during the session explicitly supported carbon pricing and associated revenues, compared with 17, predominantly oil-producing states, opposing the mechanism.

The framework could generate an estimated $10bn-$15bn annually, with revenues intended to reward early adoption of zero- and near-zero-emission fuels and support a just transition, particularly in developing countries.

However, plenty remains unresolved. UCL analysis suggested the initial global fuel intensity reduction pathway could be softened around 2030 before becoming considerably steeper towards 2040. Proposals covering rewards, surplus-unit trading and compliance mechanisms also remain under negotiation.

Japan’s proposal to replace centralised GHG pricing with shipowner-directed contributions gained little traction, while China’s suggestion that compliance payments and rewards could be netted into a single transaction attracted broader support.

“The devil is still in the detail,” UCL’s Shipping and Oceans Research Group cautioned, noting that several important elements remained wide open despite a more cooperative atmosphere.

Jesse Fahnestock, director of decarbonisation at the Global Maritime Forum, said member states had shown “a continued willingness to find common ground”, but warned that ambition must remain sufficient to underpin long-term investment in zero-emission shipping.

Negotiators now face an extremely compressed timetable. The next technical working group meets from November 23 to 27, immediately followed by MEPC 85 from November 30 to December 3. The extraordinary MEPC session that was adjourned last year is scheduled to resume on December 4.

The Net-Zero Framework was agreed in principle in April 2025, only for its adoption to be delayed following intense US and Saudi opposition.

text:
Environmental non-profit Pacific Environment and Nanyang Technological University, Singapore (NTU Singapore) have issued a new study highlighting that strict and reliable fuel certification is essential to keep the global shipping industry's transition to clean fuels honest and fraud-free.

The study titled "The role of sustainable fuels certification schemes in maritime decarbonisation", was led by the Maritime Energy & Sustainable Development Centre of Excellence (MESD) at NTU Singapore.

It evaluates established certification systems - including those by the International Sustainability & Carbon Certification (ISCC) and Roundtable on Sustainable Biomaterials (RSB), Brazil's RenovaBio, the California Air Resources Board's Low Carbon Fuel Standard (CARB LCFS), and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's Renewable Fuel Standard (U.S. EPA RFS) - to guide the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) as it establishes global standards for Sustainable Fuel Certification Schemes (SFCS).

These existing frameworks provide critical blueprints for measuring full-lifecycle carbon emissions, tracking fuel ownership, and ensuring broader environmental sustainability.

Singapore climate specialist, Lim Jie Ying, Pacific Environment, said, "Certification systems will play an essential role in ensuring that zero- and near-zero-emission fuels deliver genuine environmental benefits. As shipping scales up the use of these fuels, we need certification systems that are robust enough to guard against fraud and unsustainable production, while also being practical and workable across complex international supply chains."

The study outlines major gaps in global fuel supply chains that leave them vulnerable to cheating. For example, documented cases of fraud involving recycled waste, such as used cooking oil and palm oil mill effluent, demonstrate the limitations of verification systems relying purely on paper documentation without physical origin checks.

To tackle these risks, the study recommends chemical testing or fuel "fingerprinting" to verify fuel authenticity independently, alongside stronger cross-checks. It also calls for a centralised digital database to log all fuel transactions, preventing suppliers from falsely claiming the same batch of green fuel more than once.

Lead researcher of the study, Dr Yeoh Keat Ping, Research Lead at MESD, NTU Singapore, said: "Strengthening the traceability of sustainable fuels through continued research and innovation will be critical in supporting the maritime energy transition. This requires a combined effort across policy formulation, laboratory validation, digital tools and shared industry knowledge. As traded volumes of sustainable fuels grow, these solutions must be robust enough to keep pace with an evolving landscape."

Additionally, the study addresses the risk of Indirect Land-Use Change (ILUC), where clearing land for fuel crops causes deforestation and displaces food production elsewhere. It urges the IMO to adopt a balanced risk-based approach to cap- or phase-out high-risk crop feedstocks, protecting both ecosystems and global food security.

For Singapore, Pacific Environment notes that the study highlights a key opportunity to strengthen the country's role as a trusted green maritime hub. By expanding training for local sustainability auditors and adopting fuel fingerprinting techniques, Singapore could ensure high supply chain integrity for alternative fuels moving through Southeast Asia.

text:
LNG bunker industry body SEA-LNG said last week's ISWG-GHG 22 meeting showed member states were more open to finding a workable compromise on the Net-Zero Framework (NZF).

The meeting in London marked SEA-LNG’s first participation at the IMO as an accredited participant, it said in a press release on Monday.

The discussions covered five areas: GHG Fuel Intensity (GFI) calculation and certification, the GFI reduction pathway, compliance approaches, a possible fund or facility, and zero- or near-zero-emission (ZNZ) rewards.

SEA-LNG said the debate showed “how difficult the negotiation remains” but also “how much it has matured”.

On technology, the organisation said neutrality was “becoming even more important”, with onboard carbon capture and storage (OCCS) moving into the GFI discussion.

SEA-LNG also highlighted growing discussion around compliance flexibility, including surplus units, pooling, borrowing and netting.

It said solutions should remain “fuel agnostic and practical and realistic”

The organisation said the fund debate was becoming “less binary” and increasingly focused on what functions were needed, how they would be financed and what role the IMO should play.

On methane, SEA-LNG said the pathway “remains firmly part of the conversation”, pointing to sustainable biomethane and synthetic methane.

It added that the debate was now “more specific, more informed and more grounded in the practical realities of implementation” than it was two years ago.

“The direction of travel is still not clear,” SEA-LNG said.

“But there is more openness today to finding a workable compromise than there was six months ago.”

text:
Classification society DNV on Tuesday (8 September) said it has signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Garden Reach Shipbuilders and Engineers Limited (GRSE) for a new strategic collaboration on advanced shipbuilding, digitalization, green technologies and competence development.

The MoU, aimed at supporting the growth of India’s maritime and defence sectors, was signed at the SMM trade fair in Hamburg last week.

Under the agreement, DNV will support GRSE by providing classification and technical advice on naval, defence, and specialized vessels as well as offering regulatory insights on evolving maritime regulations and international naval standards.

The collaboration will cover areas including modular construction, design optimization, and the development of advanced vessels such as autonomous platforms, next-generation offshore patrol vessels and polar research vessels. DNV will also provide advisory support to help enhance GRSE’s repair and refit infrastructure to serve both domestic and international naval clients.

In addition, the two organizations will also collaborate on the development of electric and hybrid propulsion ferries, low-carbon naval auxiliary vessels, and pathways for alternative fuels including hydrogen and ammonia. The agreement further includes lifecycle emissions assessments and support for compliance with Maritime Amrit Kaal Vision 2047, and international environmental standards.

Knut Ørbeck-Nilssen, DNV CEO, said: “Shipbuilders are being asked to make long-term decisions against a backdrop of geopolitical tension and market unpredictability, and that uncertainty is one of the biggest concerns we hear across the industry.

“But this also creates opportunities for innovation and to develop new capabilities, across the whole maritime value chain. We have a relationship with Indian shipping and shipbuilding that spans more than five decades now, are very pleased to be working with a future focussed partner like GRSE as they work to develop advanced shipbuilding design, processes and systems for customers locally and abroad.”

Cmde P R Hari, Chairman and Managing Director, GRSE, said: “This is a partnership focused on innovation, sustainability and global excellence – contributing to a stronger and more self-reliant Indian maritime and defence ecosystem.”

DNV will also contribute its expertise in areas such as AI-enabled ship design, digital twins and cybersecurity. The partners will also run joint training programs for GRSE professionals, Indian naval architects and surveyors, working to strengthen India’s maritime supply chain and building capacity particularly for the Eastern Indian maritime cluster.

Clean energy equipment and services provider CIMC Enric on Monday (7 September) said China’s first green methanol bunkering operation for a bulk carrier was completed at Guangzhou anchorage.

The company said the bunkering operation also marked the first bio-methanol STS bunkering operation at Guangzhou Port.

A total of 1,021 metric tonnes (mt) of bio-methanol was supplied ship-to-ship (STS) to the world’s first methanol dual-fuel Ultramax bulk carrier.

The operation was completed on 6 September by China Shipping & Sinopec Suppliers Co Ltd’s Da Qing 268, which carried bio-methanol produced at CIMC Enric’s green methanol facility in Zhanjiang.

The successful operation in Guangzhou, following previous green methanol bunkering operations in Shenzhen and Hong Kong, means that Guangdong-produced bio-based methanol has established a supply network across the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area.

The company said the development connects the production, storage, transportation and bunkering segments of the green methanol supply chain, moving the region beyond individual pilot projects towards coordinated operations across the Greater Bay Area.

CIMC Enric described its Zhanjiang green methanol facility as China’s first commercial-scale bio-methanol production plant.

Since beginning production, the Zhanjiang facility has maintained a stable production and delivery schedule, supplying bio-based methanol to major ports across China, with delivery volumes continuing to increase, according to the company.

The first phase of the facility has an annual production capacity of 50,000 metric tonnes (mt), while its methanol products have a carbon emission reduction rate of more than 85%, CIMC Enric said.

The products have also obtained ISCC EU sustainability certification, with the company saying their specifications meet international requirements for shipping decarbonisation and can support the low-carbon operation of vessels.

International energy terminal operator KN Energies on Tuesday (8 September) said bunker vessel Titan Vision arrived at the Klaipėda LNG terminal on the same day for the vessel’s first LNG reloading operation in Klaipėda.

title: Ammonia Shipping Fuel Could Spike Ocean Nitrogen 185 Percent; IMO Framework Doesn't Cover It
description:
Current global anthropogenic reactive nitrogen emissions already stand at approximately 210 teragrams of nitrogen per year.
Frequently Asked Questions Is ammonia shipping fuel actually better for the environment than conventional fuel?
Why does burning ammonia cause ocean nitrogen pollution if ammonia contains no carbon?
The planetary nitrogen boundary — the level of reactive nitrogen creation beyond which Earth's systems begin entering unsafe conditions — is 62 to 82 teragrams of nitrogen per year.
Current global anthropogenic reactive nitrogen emissions are approximately 210 Tg N/yr: already two and a half to three times over the safe limit.
text:
The shipping industry's pivot to ammonia as a zero-carbon fuel could worsen ocean nitrogen pollution by up to 185 percent compared to the fuel oil it replaces — threatening coral reef bleaching, coastal dead zones, and even the fuel's own climate benefit — unless regulators close major gaps in the certification framework governing ammonia's entire production and combustion chain, according to a peer-reviewed systematic review published Monday in Frontiers in Marine Science.

The study, the first to trace reactive nitrogen through the complete ammonia marine fuel supply chain — from production facility to combustion exhaust to atmospheric deposition into the sea — arrives at a critical moment. The International Maritime Organization is actively accelerating ammonia fuel adoption as the backbone of its 2050 net-zero shipping strategy, and ammonia-fueled vessel deliveries are scaling rapidly through the late 2020s, locking in hull and engine specifications that will operate for 25 to 30 years.

Ammonia Fuel Is Carbon-Free — Not Impact-Free

Maritime shipping carries more than 80 percent of world trade by volume and accounts for roughly three percent of global carbon dioxide emissions. Ammonia — particularly "green" ammonia produced from renewable electricity — has emerged as a frontrunner alternative fuel because it contains no carbon, making its combustion nominally free of CO2. Some projections see ammonia capturing 35 to 60 percent of the marine fuel market by 2050 in net-zero scenarios.

But the authors of the new review, drawn from Environmental Defense Fund Europe, Opportunity Green in London, and One Planet Port in Rotterdam, argue that the industry and its regulators have been asking the wrong question. The issue is not only what comes out of the smokestack in terms of carbon — it is what happens to the reactive nitrogen compounds that ammonia combustion releases into a global ocean already under severe nitrogen stress.

Burning ammonia in a ship's engine does not produce CO2, but it does produce nitrogen oxides (NOx), nitrous oxide (N2O), and unreacted ammonia that escapes as "slip" from incomplete combustion. These reactive nitrogen species, once airborne, are transported by wind and deposited onto ocean surfaces — sometimes hundreds of kilometers from the ship itself — where they enter the marine nitrogen cycle and trigger a chain of ecological consequences.

The critical finding is how much the outcome depends on what regulatory controls are in place. Under stringent controls — renewable-based ammonia production, low NOx and N2O emissions from engines, minimal ammonia slip, and full boil-off gas capture — total reactive nitrogen emissions from the ammonia fuel chain could be approximately 66 percent lower than current very-low-sulfur fuel oil for the same energy output. Without those controls, they could be up to 185 percent higher.

What Gets Into the Ocean, and Why It Matters

The mechanism is what researchers call the "nitrogen cascade" — a concept first described by University of Virginia biogeochemist John Galloway and colleagues in a foundational 2003 paper in BioScience — in which a single molecule of reactive nitrogen released at one point in the industrial system can produce ecological damage across atmospheric, aquatic, and marine environments before finally returning to inert nitrogen gas.

For ammonia marine fuel, the cascade operates in four linked stages: production, storage and bunkering, shipboard combustion, and atmospheric transport to ocean deposition. Nitrogen losses occur at every stage, not just from the engine exhaust that previous emissions analyses have focused on.

The ecological consequences depend sharply on where the nitrogen lands. The study identifies five ocean environments that together cover vast areas of the global ocean and sit directly along the world's busiest shipping corridors.

Oligotrophic gyres — the vast, nutrient-starved subtropical ocean zones covering roughly 40 percent of the global ocean surface — have adapted over millions of years to near-zero nitrogen availability. Even modest nitrogen enrichment from shipping corridors crossing the North Pacific and North Atlantic subtropical gyres could shift phytoplankton communities toward larger, less efficient organisms, disrupting carbon cycling in ways that are poorly understood.

Coral reef systems are acutely sensitive because coral-zooxanthellae symbiosis functions optimally under nitrogen-limited conditions. Experimental and field studies show that chronic nitrogen enrichment of just 1 to 3 micromolar — concentrations achievable through atmospheric deposition from intensified ammonia shipping — can reduce coral cover, increase macroalgal abundance, elevate disease prevalence, and lower thermal bleaching thresholds by 0.5 to 1.0°C (0.9 to 1.8°F). Reef systems most directly in the path of major shipping lanes — the Caribbean reefs adjacent to the Panama Canal, the Red Sea along the Suez route, and the offshore Great Barrier Reef region — face compounding risk as marine heatwaves grow more frequent. Elevated nitrogen can degrade reefs that survive warming events they otherwise would have withstood.

Oxygen minimum zones (OMZs) represent the most alarming interaction. These oxygen-depleted ocean regions occupy roughly 8 percent of ocean volume yet account for 30 to 50 percent of global oceanic nitrogen loss and roughly half of marine nitrous oxide production. When reactive nitrogen deposited from ammonia-fueled ships reaches OMZ waters and stimulates surface productivity, the sinking organic matter is broken down by microbes through a pathway that generates N2O as a byproduct.

The climate implication is severe. Nitrous oxide is a greenhouse gas 273 times as potent as CO2 over 100 years, and a major ozone-depleting substance. The study finds that under weak emissions controls, these indirect N2O formation pathways could offset 15 to 40 percent of ammonia fuel's projected climate benefit. High-density shipping corridors overlap directly with the major OMZs at highest risk: the Arabian Sea, the eastern tropical Pacific, the Bay of Bengal, and the southwestern African margin.

Marginal and semi-enclosed seas — the Baltic, Mediterranean, Black, East China, Yellow, and South China Seas — are already under intense pressure from agricultural runoff and urban wastewater. The Baltic Sea alone receives 600,000 to 800,000 metric tons of nitrogen annually, far exceeding its assimilative capacity, with oxygen-depleted dead zones covering 60,000 to 100,000 square kilometers (23,000 to 38,600 square miles) of seabed. Shipping already contributes 20 to 25 percent of atmospheric nitrogen deposition in the Baltic and North Sea regions. Additional ammonia-fuel-related deposition could compound conditions in systems that have zero remaining assimilative capacity.

East Asian marginal seas — covering a region that supports roughly 20 percent of global fish catch — already receive shipping-derived nitrogen at 15 to 25 percent of atmospheric deposition, depending on proximity to major ports.

Why the Engine Can't Fix It Alone

Understanding why existing emissions frameworks miss this risk requires understanding how ammonia combustion works at the engine level — and where the critical tradeoffs emerge.

Dual-fuel internal combustion engines, the technology currently being deployed in the first wave of ammonia-powered ships, combust ammonia with a small hydrocarbon pilot charge for ignition. Untreated NOx emissions from these engines range from 2 to 9 grams of NOx per megajoule of energy delivered, comparable to or exceeding conventional heavy fuel oil at approximately 4.7 g/MJ. The fuel-bound nitrogen pathway in ammonia combustion substitutes for the thermal NOx that would otherwise be partially limited by ammonia's lower flame temperature.

Ammonia also presents fundamental combustion challenges: its laminar flame speed is just 7 centimeters per second — compared to 37 cm/s for liquefied natural gas — and its auto-ignition temperature is 651°C (1,204°F) versus 580°C (1,076°F) for diesel. These properties mean incomplete combustion is structurally more likely than with conventional fuels, with ammonia slip ranging from less than 0.5 percent to 2 to 5 percent of fuel mass depending on operating conditions.

The governing constraint is a tradeoff that makes single-pollutant optimization actively counterproductive: measures that reduce NOx (lower combustion temperatures) increase ammonia slip; measures that reduce slip (higher temperatures, leaner mixtures) increase NOx. Selective catalytic reduction systems that cut NOx to below IMO Tier III compliance levels (0.5 g NOx/MJ) can simultaneously increase ammonia slip unless a downstream ammonia-slip catalyst (ASC) is also deployed. An integrated SCR+ASC system addresses both pollutants simultaneously — but the study documents that no current regulatory framework mandates this integrated approach.

Nitrogen also exits the system through a route that existing governance frameworks specifically do not address: exhaust gas treatment effluent. Scrubber systems that capture nitrogen from engine exhaust transfer it into nitrogen-bearing wastewater streams that are then discharged into port waters. This shifts the pollution from the atmosphere to the sea, but maritime discharge rules do not currently treat nitrogen-bearing effluent as a regulated waste stream under any major international instrument.

Planetary Nitrogen Boundary Already Exceeded

The study places the ammonia marine fuel governance gap in the context of a larger Earth-system problem that makes the stakes higher than they might otherwise appear.

Current global anthropogenic reactive nitrogen emissions already stand at approximately 210 teragrams of nitrogen per year. The planetary boundary for reactive nitrogen — the level beyond which Earth's nitrogen cycle begins producing unsafe conditions for human civilization — is 62 to 82 Tg N/yr. The current system is already operating at roughly two and a half to three times the safe boundary before a single ammonia-fueled ship leaves port.

Ammonia marine fuel demand could require expanding global ammonia production by three to four times its current level of approximately 185 million metric tons per year by mid-century, layered on top of existing agricultural production that is not projected to decline. This expansion would add concentrated reactive nitrogen sources around industrial production hubs, ports, and shipping corridors in a nitrogen cycle with zero remaining margin.

The study draws an explicit historical parallel. Ammonia's role as an agricultural fertilizer over the past century drove one of the most significant anthropogenic perturbations of any Earth system boundary. The downstream nitrogen losses from fertilizer use were largely uncontrolled for decades despite being technically avoidable. "The pervasive inefficiencies identified in agricultural Nr use a generation ago have an analogue in the projected ammonia marine fuel value chain," the study notes, "where leakage and combustion losses vary by more than an order of magnitude depending on technology and operational practice."

Does the IMO Know, and What Comes Next?

Current IMO instruments governing marine emissions — MARPOL Annex VI, the IGF Code for low-flashpoint fuels, and SOLAS — were designed for fossil-fuel shipping and focus on CO2, sulfur oxides, and conventional NOx. The IMO's own Net-Zero Framework, still under discussion as of this writing, focuses on greenhouse gas intensity without requiring lifecycle reactive nitrogen accounting.

Ammonia certification schemes — including ISCC, Ammonia Europe, and CertifHY — focus almost exclusively on GHG intensity, leaving nitrogen cascade impacts entirely unaccounted for. At the EU level, FuelEU Maritime sets declining GHG intensity targets for shipping, and the EU Emissions Trading System prices CO2, but neither addresses nitrogen.

The study identifies the 2026 to 2028 period as a decisive window to establish frameworks before large-scale ammonia fuel infrastructure becomes entrenched. Ships ordered and built in this period will operate for 25 to 30 years. If high-emission propulsion systems become the norm before regulations catch up, retrofitting the global fleet would be technically complex and economically prohibitive.

What Regulators Must Do

What the study's authors say needs to happen:

Lifecycle accounting for reactive nitrogen — not just CO2 — must be embedded in certification and compliance frameworks covering production, bunkering, combustion, and downstream effluent. Integrated emission controls at the engine level must address NOx, ammonia slip, and N2O simultaneously rather than optimizing for any one species in isolation. Geographic differentiation in environmental standards must reflect the reality that the same tonne of nitrogen deposited over an oligotrophic gyre, a coral reef, or an oxygen minimum zone can produce vastly different ecological damage. Renewable-based ammonia production must be a prerequisite for vessels claiming climate benefit, since coal-based "black" and fossil-fuel "grey" ammonia pathways emit NOx at rates 20 to 45 times higher per tonne than renewable electrolysis-based pathways.

Is Ammonia Fuel Worth Pursuing?

Ammonia remains a credible path to decarbonizing shipping — but only under conditions that do not yet uniformly exist in the regulatory frameworks governing its adoption. The study's authors do not argue against ammonia fuel. They argue that realizing its climate benefits without triggering a parallel nitrogen crisis in the world's oceans requires governance that current certification schemes do not provide.

The outcome is not predetermined by chemistry. Under stringent controls and renewable production pathways, ammonia marine fuel can deliver substantial climate benefits and reduce nitrogen emissions relative to the diesel-era fleet it replaces. Under weak controls and fossil-fuel-derived ammonia production, it becomes a dual crisis: one that fails to deliver the climate benefit it promised and adds a new anthropogenic burden to ocean ecosystems already operating past their safe limits.

Whether that governance materializes in the window before large-scale ammonia fuel infrastructure is entrenched is, the study suggests, the defining policy question of the maritime energy transition.

The study, "Beyond Carbon: Reactive Nitrogen Emissions from Ammonia as a Marine Fuel and Implications for Ocean Ecosystems," was authored by Lucy Gilliam, James Kershaw, Stavroula S. Sartzetakis, Marie Cabbia Hubatova, and Sofia Esquivel-Elizondo, and published September 8, 2026, in Frontiers in Marine Science (DOI: 10.3389/fmars.2026.1907733). It was funded in part by Environmental Defense Fund.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is ammonia shipping fuel actually better for the environment than conventional fuel?

It depends entirely on the emissions controls and production pathway in place. Under stringent controls — renewable electrolysis-based ammonia, integrated NOx and ammonia-slip catalysts, and full boil-off gas capture — a new systematic review published in Frontiers in Marine Science finds ammonia marine fuel could reduce reactive nitrogen emissions by approximately 66 percent compared to current very-low-sulfur fuel oil. Without those controls, the same fuel could increase nitrogen emissions by up to 185 percent. The outcome is determined by governance, not chemistry.

Why does burning ammonia cause ocean nitrogen pollution if ammonia contains no carbon?

Because ammonia's chemical formula is NH3 — it contains nitrogen but no carbon. When burned in a ship's engine, that nitrogen does not disappear: it is released as nitrogen oxides (NOx), nitrous oxide (N2O), and unreacted ammonia slip escaping from incomplete combustion. These reactive nitrogen compounds travel through the atmosphere and deposit onto ocean surfaces hundreds of kilometers from the ship, where they enter the marine nitrogen cycle and can trigger eutrophication, coral reef degradation, and the production of additional N2O — a greenhouse gas 273 times as potent as CO2 — in low-oxygen ocean waters.

What does shipping nitrogen pollution mean for coral reefs specifically?

Coral-zooxanthellae symbiosis — the partnership between coral animals and the algae that give reefs their color and productivity — functions optimally under nitrogen-limited conditions. Research shows that chronic nitrogen enrichment of just 1 to 3 micromolar concentrations can reduce coral cover, increase competing macroalgae, and lower thermal bleaching thresholds by 0.5 to 1.0°C (0.9 to 1.8°F). This interaction with warming is the most consequential pathway: even modest nitrogen increases from ammonia shipping corridors could accelerate reef degradation during marine heatwaves that would otherwise be survivable.

What is the planetary nitrogen boundary, and why does it matter for this debate?

The planetary nitrogen boundary — the level of reactive nitrogen creation beyond which Earth's systems begin entering unsafe conditions — is 62 to 82 teragrams of nitrogen per year. Current global anthropogenic reactive nitrogen emissions are approximately 210 Tg N/yr: already two and a half to three times over the safe limit. Expanding global ammonia production three to four times over by mid-century to supply marine fuel would add a massive new nitrogen source to a cycle already operating without margin. This context means the worst-case scenario for uncontrolled ammonia fuel is not merely a risk to be weighed against benefits — it is a compounding burden on a system that is already past its planetary safety threshold.

title: Cyprus, Greece, Malta and Italy unite over future of EU shipping

text:
Cyprus, Greece, Malta and Italy have agreed to strengthen their common front on European shipping, signing a joint declaration in Limassol on Wednesday as they seek greater influence over decisions on competitiveness and decarbonisation in Brussels and at the International Maritime Organisation (IMO).

The agreement came at the ninth maritime meeting between Cyprus, Greece and Malta, held for the first time in an expanded 3+1 format with Italy, bringing together four Mediterranean countries with some of the EU’s strongest shipping interests.

Cyprus Shipping Deputy Minister Marina Hadjimanolis hosted Greece’s Maritime Affairs and Insular Policy Minister Vassilis Kikilias and Malta’s Minister for Sustainable Mobility Chris Bonett at the Parklane Hotel in Limassol.

Italy’s Deputy Minister for Infrastructure and Transport Edoardo Rixi participated online, while Italy was represented at the meeting in Limassol by Ambassador Antonella Cavallari.

Cavallari has served as Italy’s ambassador to Cyprus since January 2026.

Speaking after the meeting, Hadjimanolis said the declaration reflected what she described as common concerns over the future and competitiveness of European shipping, alongside the challenge of decarbonising the industry.

She said the four countries had agreed that acting together could deliver better results and give their concerns greater weight when decisions affecting all 27 EU member states are taken.

At the same time, Hadjimanolis stressed that the cooperation was not intended to undermine wider European unity.

“The unity of the European Union is important,” she said, explaining that some maritime issues nevertheless affected certain member states more directly than others.

As four major maritime nations, she added, Cyprus, Greece, Malta and Italy were “ready to lead together this change”.

The declaration therefore gives the four governments a common platform as discussions intensify over the future regulatory framework for European shipping.

That coordination is expected to focus particularly on the negotiations taking place at the IMO over international decarbonisation measures and on the forthcoming revision of the EU Emissions Trading System for shipping.

The Greek Shipping Ministry confirmed ahead of the meeting that both issues would be given particular attention in Limassol, alongside closer coordination between the four governments with the aim of safeguarding European shipping competitiveness.

Kikilias, meanwhile, placed much of the emphasis on the relationship between shipping policy and the cost of living for European households.

He said the discussions on European competitiveness in shipping were closely linked to the wider economy and “to everyday life for our European families”.

Inflation, energy costs and food prices, he argued, could all be affected by decisions taken over shipping, energy, shipyards and ports in the coming years.

For that reason, he said, such decisions should not be considered separately from their economic consequences.

Kikilias said European policies had to be approached “realistically and practically”, particularly during a period marked by geopolitical tension and instability.

Governments, he added, had to do everything within their power “to support our people”.

The Greek minister described Wednesday’s agreement as an important step in that effort and expressed hope that other member states would eventually join the initiative.

He argued that the four-country position was based on “reason”, “logic” and “balance”, with the aim of securing the best possible outcome for both European shipping and European consumers.

Bonett similarly stressed that the cooperation should not be seen simply as four governments protecting their own shipping industries.

Although Cyprus, Greece, Malta and Italy share both their Mediterranean geography and strong maritime sectors, he said the issues under discussion affect Europe as a whole and international trade more broadly.

Energy supplies and much of the goods consumed by European economies arrive by sea, he noted, while for island states in particular maritime transport is not simply one transport option among many.

“For some of us, we don’t have a choice, because the sea is practically our neighbourhood,” Bonett said.

The Maltese minister said the four countries therefore had an obligation to ensure that the regulatory decisions taken for shipping remained workable.

Among the pressures facing the sector, he pointed to the geopolitical situation and decarbonisation.

Bonett made clear that the countries supported the move towards cutting emissions, describing decarbonisation as a choice made to protect the planet for future generations.

However, he warned that the transition could not be pursued without considering its impact on the wider economy.

“Modernising, decarbonising, innovation should not come at the cost of businesses and families,” he said.

That, according to Bonett, was one of the most important messages contained in the declaration signed on Wednesday.

The four countries want to work more closely and support each other, while convincing the wider EU that their position could ultimately benefit the continent rather than only their respective national industries.

Bonett said policy therefore “has to make sense” and “has to be pragmatic”.

The coming weeks and months would be particularly important, he added, as the countries reiterate their common position in European discussions.

Shipping also needed a regulatory environment which did not produce avoidable increases in costs for consumers, he said.

The issue has become particularly important as the EU ETS reaches its full phase-in for shipping.

Under the system, shipping companies were required to surrender allowances covering 40 per cent of applicable emissions for 2024 and 70 per cent for 2025, while the requirement reaches 100 per cent in 2026.

Methane and nitrous oxide emissions are also included in the maritime ETS from this year, alongside carbon dioxide.

The European Commission has also begun work on a wider revision of the EU ETS, proposing changes in July aimed at reconciling the bloc’s climate objectives with industrial competitiveness.

For Mediterranean shipping countries, however, one of the recurring concerns is that European environmental rules can create a competitive difference between ports inside and immediately outside the EU.

That point was picked up directly by Cavallari.

The Italian ambassador said Italy regarded participation in the group as particularly important because of the collective weight carried by the four states.

“The four of us together account for 75 per cent of the entire European Union fleet,” she said, describing the figure as “very meaningful”.

The four countries should therefore use their combined position, she argued, to raise their priorities and concerns more effectively within the EU.

Cavallari nevertheless echoed Hadjimanolis in stressing that the approach was not intended to divide the bloc.

European unity remained important, she said, but it was also useful for Mediterranean member states to bring their own perspective into the debate because they shared similar values, priorities and concerns.

A central part of that position was the need to reconcile competitiveness with decarbonisation.

Cavallari said it was important “to put together competitiveness and decarbonisation” and ensure that climate regulation did not jeopardise the shipping industry.

Referring to Rixi’s intervention during the meeting, she said the Italian deputy minister had underlined the importance of taking the needs and priorities of the industry into consideration in the interests of the wider EU.

Most goods move at some stage by sea, she noted, meaning the economic implications of shipping policy spread well beyond the industry itself.

The ambassador also drew attention to competition between Mediterranean ports.

“There are a number of ports in the Mediterranean, some of them are European, some are not,” she said.

Different regulatory requirements could therefore create problems for European shipping businesses when competing with operators using neighbouring non-EU ports.

The four countries wanted to ensure that EU regulations did not place their industries at a structural disadvantage to competitors operating immediately outside the bloc.

Cavallari linked that issue directly to Europe’s strategic autonomy and competitiveness, saying cooperation between the four Mediterranean countries ultimately served wider European interests.

The European Commission itself has increasingly placed those two objectives alongside the green transition.

In March, it adopted its Industrial Maritime Strategy together with a new ports strategy, arguing that shipping, shipbuilding and ports are central to Europe’s trade, security and strategic autonomy.

The Commission said European shipping represents more than one third of global shipping tonnage, while the industry faces intensifying international competition as well as growing costs linked to the energy transition.

European ports, meanwhile, handle around 74 per cent of the EU’s external trade and approximately 3.4 billion tonnes of goods annually.

Cavallari said the four-country cooperation should also extend beyond European institutions.

International bodies such as the IMO were equally important, she said, and acting jointly would make it easier for the Mediterranean countries to ensure their views were heard.

“We have to speak louder also internationally,” she said.

That international dimension comes only days after another round of negotiations at the IMO on its proposed global framework for reducing greenhouse gas emissions from ships.

The IMO’s Intersessional Working Group on greenhouse gas emissions met in London from September 1 to 4, considering concerns raised over the proposed amendments to Marpol Annex VI forming part of the organisation’s Net-Zero Framework.

Although delegates made progress, a number of matters remain unresolved and governments were invited to continue consultations ahead of the next round of negotiations.

The next working group meeting will take place from November 23 to 27, immediately before the Marine Environment Protection Committee meets from November 30 to December 3.

That timetable gives Wednesday’s agreement additional significance, as Cyprus, Greece, Malta and Italy now have only a matter of weeks to coordinate positions before negotiations resume.

Bonett also used his remarks to emphasise another principle which has become increasingly significant during the current period of geopolitical instability.

The “main cardinal principle of shipping”, he said, was that merchant ships must have the right to free and safe passage wherever they operate.

He called on countries involved in conflicts to pursue dialogue, arguing that uninterrupted and peaceful trade was essential both for consumers and for the global economy.

The meeting itself also represents a further development of a maritime cooperation mechanism which has existed between Cyprus, Greece and Malta for years.

Wednesday’s gathering was the ninth meeting under the framework and marked the first time Italy participated.

It was also the first time Cyprus hosted the format since 2018, when the island held the sixth meeting, while the previous gathering took place in Greece in 2023.

Ahead of the meeting, Hadjimanolis had described Italy’s participation as the result of targeted efforts to broaden Cyprus’ regional maritime partnerships, saying closer coordination was increasingly necessary as shipping faced major regulatory and geopolitical challenges.

Cavallari said Wednesday’s declaration would not mark the end of the initiative.

The four countries had also agreed to continue meeting, she said, with further gatherings expected.

At the same time, Rixi had encouraged the group to reach out to other potential partners within Europe and beyond, particularly countries which shared similar views and could support the group’s approach in international negotiations.

For the four Mediterranean states, the aim is therefore not simply to create another regional forum, but to build a bloc capable of carrying greater weight as Europe decides how quickly shipping should decarbonise, who should bear the cost and how EU operators can remain competitive against rivals outside the bloc.

As Hadjimanolis put it after the meeting, there may be questions which affect certain member states more than others, but European unity remains the objective.

The message from Limassol was that Cyprus, Greece, Malta and Italy intend to make sure Europe’s major maritime states have a stronger voice in deciding how that objective is achieved.

title: EU ETS overhaul: What the Commission's proposal means for shipping - SAFETY4SEA
description:
Maritime transport has been included in the EU ETS since January 2024.
The system covers 100% of emissions from voyages between EU ports and emissions within EU ports, as well as 50% of emissions from voyages between EU and non-EU ports.
Under the Commission’s proposed revision, dedicated support would be provided for sustainable maritime fuels and eligible zero-emission propulsion technologies.
The proposal also seeks to reduce the risk of shipping companies lowering ETS liabilities through calls at nearby non-EU ports.
Industry organisations have welcomed the stronger focus on maritime decarbonisation but argue that further improvements are needed.
text:
For shipping, the proposal combines greater support for decarbonisation with tighter safeguards against evasion and efforts to simplify compliance.

Maritime transport has been included in the EU ETS since January 2024. The system covers 100% of emissions from voyages between EU ports and emissions within EU ports, as well as 50% of emissions from voyages between EU and non-EU ports.

Following the phase-in period, emissions generated in 2026 are subject to a 100% surrender requirement, with the corresponding allowances surrendered in 2027. Methane and nitrous oxide are also included alongside CO₂ from 2026.

Under the Commission’s proposed revision, dedicated support would be provided for sustainable maritime fuels and eligible zero-emission propulsion technologies.

More broadly, an Industrial Decarbonisation Bank would support industrial transition, while Member States would be required to direct 50% of national ETS revenues towards decarbonising sectors covered by the system.

The proposal also seeks to reduce the risk of shipping companies lowering ETS liabilities through calls at nearby non-EU ports.

Such practices could result in liability being calculated on a shorter final leg into the EU rather than a longer voyage, reducing compliance costs without necessarily reducing overall emissions.

Existing anti-evasion provisions already apply to designated neighbouring container transhipment ports, including East Port Said and Tanger Med.

The proposed revision would broaden the criteria for identifying neighbouring transhipment ports, including certain ports within 150 nautical miles of the EU, while increasing the frequency with which the Commission reviews the list.

In addition, the Commission proposes extending the ETS to certain categories of smaller vessels between 400 and 5,000 gross tonnage, extending existing maritime derogations to 2035, and strengthening the review clause to address the risk of double payments if a global market-based measure is adopted through the IMO.

Industry organisations have welcomed the stronger focus on maritime decarbonisation but argue that further improvements are needed. The World Shipping Council notes that sustainable maritime fuels can cost 100–400% more than conventional marine fuels and supports reinvesting ETS revenues to help close that gap.

At the same time, it has raised concerns that expanded transhipment rules could affect the competitiveness of neighbouring non-EU ports.

European Shipowners | ECSA similarly considers the proposed allocation of 110 million allowances- worth approximately €10 billion – only an initial step compared with the estimated €90 billion the sector could contribute to the system between 2030 and 2040.

It is calling for broader support for sustainable fuels, energy-efficiency projects and clean technologies.

The central challenge remains ensuring that carbon pricing delivers measurable emissions reductions without distorting shipping networks, shifting activity outside EU jurisdiction or creating overlapping regional and global costs.

The linked revision of the EU MRV and FuelEU Maritime rules is also relevant. The Commission proposes a single monitoring and reporting workflow covering MRV, EU ETS and FuelEU Maritime, with estimated annual savings of 10–20% of current MRV administrative compliance costs.

The proposals remain subject to negotiations between the European Parliament and Council, with the streamlined framework proposed to apply from 2029.

title: Global Shipping Industry Facing Unprecedented Maritime Crises: IMO - RTT News
description:
The global shipping industry is facing a "genuinely unprecedented" convergence of maritime crises, with vessels and seafarers increasingly used as "leverage" in conflicts, a top official at the UN's International Maritime Organization said.
Four regions - the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea, the waters off Somalia, and the Black Sea - are now simultaneously active theaters of danger, on a scale the shipping industry has not seen before.
Vessels and seafarers are being trapped and attacked in conflicts that have nothing to do with the ships themselves.
This is the first time so many vessels and seafarers have been threatened across multiple regions at once.
Perhaps the deepest concern is the future of the seafaring workforce itself as without seafarers there is no shipping industry.
text:
The global shipping industry is facing a "genuinely unprecedented" convergence of maritime crises, with vessels and seafarers increasingly used as "leverage" in conflicts, a top official at the UN's International Maritime Organization said.

Four regions - the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea, the waters off Somalia, and the Black Sea - are now simultaneously active theaters of danger, on a scale the shipping industry has not seen before.

Vessels and seafarers are being trapped and attacked in conflicts that have nothing to do with the ships themselves.

Damien Chevalier, the Director of the Maritime Safety Division at the UN's International Maritime Organization told UN News about the scale of the threat and what's being done to protect ships and crews.

This is the first time so many vessels and seafarers have been threatened across multiple regions at once. The crisis in the Strait of Hormuz is unprecedented in terms of the number of vessels (2000) and seafarers (20,000) that were impacted at the beginning of the conflict.

The industry now faces a combination of crises: not just Hormuz, but Houthi attacks in the Red Sea and a sharp rise in piracy near Somalia, where seafarers are held hostage.

There has also been a significant increase in attacks in the Black Sea, where parties to the conflict are using drones to target oil tankers and grain-carrying vessels.

Naval assets are more focused on the threats in the Red Sea and Strait of Hormuz, and so pirates have taken the opportunity to operate, particularly against smaller, easier-to-attack bulk carriers.

A recent meeting on maritime law enforcement focused heavily on counter-piracy, given the surge in incidents and the deteriorating security situation in Somalia.

Shipping has become a deliberate instrument of geopolitical leverage, with its consequences severe and far-reaching, says Chevalier.

The Strait of Hormuz alone carries roughly 20 per cent of the world's oil, so disruption there affects inflation and living costs globally.

Both the Strait of Hormuz and the Black Sea are also critical for fertilizer and the latter for grain exports, meaning food security is at stake. The impact is likely to be felt into next year, particularly in developing countries.

While wealthier nations can draw on strategic reserves, this is only a short-term buffer; once reserves are depleted, a second wave of crisis follows. Rising shipping costs, from rerouting to added security measures, compound the problem, driving up prices on top of reduced supply.

Perhaps the deepest concern is the future of the seafaring workforce itself as without seafarers there is no shipping industry.

description:

Backed by Japan’s New Energy and Industrial Development Organisation (NEDO), J-Eng developed the engine in collaboration with Japan’s Kawasaki Heavy Industries (KHI), Yanmar, ClassNK, and Mitsui O.S.K Lines.

text:
Japan Engine Corporation (J-Eng) has completed what it claims is the first onshore operational test of a 95% hydrogen-fuelled internal combustion engine (ICE) designed for large merchant ships.

The company now plans to install the system on a 17,500-DWT vessel planned for construction by project partner Onimichi Dockyard in April 2028, when it will begin “full-scale demonstrations”.

Backed by Japan’s New Energy and Industrial Development Organisation (NEDO), J-Eng developed the engine in collaboration with Japan’s Kawasaki Heavy Industries (KHI), Yanmar, ClassNK, and Mitsui O.S.K Lines.

While the engine’s power output was not revealed, the group claimed it achieved a 95% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions versus heavy oil fuel engines.

It uses a high-pressure injection system, supplementing a small portion of a conventional fuel like diesel with hydrogen for co-firing.

Despite advances in hydrogen-fuelled maritime transport, the molecule’s role in decarbonising the sector faces questions.

Operators of larger vessels are increasingly turning to derivatives like ammonia and methanol while smaller vessels see improvements in battery-electric propulsion technology.

The International Maritime Organization plans to improve carbon levies on ships above 5,000 GT. However, adoption of its framework has been stalled since last year.

The EU already imposed carbon pricing on ships using ports within the bloc under its FuelEU Maritime legislation.

title: Poseidon Principles expands reach across marine insurance - Splash247
description:
The Poseidon Principles, the shipping finance framework banks use to track and disclose climate alignment, whose signatories represent nearly three-quarters of global shipping finance, have expanded their associate membership to include marine insurers.
Launched in 2019, the Poseidon Principles membership has historically been limited to financial institutions, providing secured credit products for vessels under the purview of the International Maritime Organization.
In 2021, several leading marine insurers recognised the opportunity to support the industry’s decarbonisation goals and launched the Poseidon Principles for Marine Insurance (PPMI), giving the insurance industry its own route to support shipping’s decarbonisation goal.
In December 2025, the Poseidon Principles broadened its membership framework, introducing a new associate membership that enabled hedge funds, private equity firms, and other institutions involved in shipping finance to engage with the initiative.
This recent expansion has presented an opportunity to bring the Poseidon Principles and PPMI together under one platform.
text:
The Poseidon Principles, the shipping finance framework banks use to track and disclose climate alignment, whose signatories represent nearly three-quarters of global shipping finance, have expanded their associate membership to include marine insurers.

The decision follows a unanimous vote by signatories at the annual meeting in May to include insurers and related organisations, including P&I clubs, brokers, reinsurers, and insurance institutions, as associate members.

This brings the financial services sector together under a single, unified platform to strengthen shipping’s decarbonisation efforts.

“The inclusion of marine insurers as associate members builds directly on the associate membership expansion we introduced at the end of last year, further reinforcing the position of the Poseidon Principles as a leading standard-setter across shipping finance and insurance,” said Paul Taylor, global head of maritime industries at Societe Generale and chair of the Poseidon Principles.

Launched in 2019, the Poseidon Principles membership has historically been limited to financial institutions, providing secured credit products for vessels under the purview of the International Maritime Organization.

In 2021, several leading marine insurers recognised the opportunity to support the industry’s decarbonisation goals and launched the Poseidon Principles for Marine Insurance (PPMI), giving the insurance industry its own route to support shipping’s decarbonisation goal.

Until now, the two initiatives have operated as distinct but closely aligned not-for-profit associations, using similar decarbonisation trajectories and calculation methods and relying on the Global Maritime Forum for secretariat services.

In December 2025, the Poseidon Principles broadened its membership framework, introducing a new associate membership that enabled hedge funds, private equity firms, and other institutions involved in shipping finance to engage with the initiative. This recent expansion has presented an opportunity to bring the Poseidon Principles and PPMI together under one platform.

“Folding PPMI into the Poseidon Principles is a natural next step to strengthen the impact of both initiatives, bringing together the expertise built on the insurance side with that of financial institutions on the lending side, an approach that is especially valuable given the current landscape facing the shipping industry,” added Patrizia Kern-Ferretti, chief insurance officer at Breeze and former chair of the PPMI.

PPMI has now officially ceased operations as a distinct entity, and former members, Cosco Shipping Captive Insurance, CTX Special Risks, Gard, Norwegian Hull Club, and Willis, have joined the Poseidon Principles as the first associate members.

In 2021, several leading marine insurers recognised the opportunity to support the industry's decarbonisation goals and came together to launch the Poseidon Principles for Marine Insurance (PPMI), giving the insurance industry its own route to support shipping's decarbonisation goal. The two initiatives have until now operated as distinct but closely aligned not-for-profit associations, using similar decarbonisation trajectories and calculation methods and relying on the Global Maritime Forum for secretariat services.

In December 2025, the Poseidon Principles broadened its membership framework, introducing a new associate membership that enabled hedge funds, private equity firms, and other institutions involved in shipping finance to engage with the initiative. This recent expansion has presented a natural opportunity to bring the Poseidon Principles and PPMI together under one platform.

"Since its inception in 2021, PPMI has developed a strong track record and methodology tailored to the insurance industry's role in shipping's decarbonisation,” said Patrizia Kern-Ferretti, Chief Insurance Officer at Breeze and former Chair of the Poseidon Principles for Marine Insurance. “Folding PPMI into the Poseidon Principles is a natural next step to strengthen the impact of both initiatives, bringing together the expertise built on the insurance side with that of financial institutions on the lending side, an approach that is especially valuable given the current landscape facing the shipping industry."

description:
A new coalition has been launched in the UK to bring together the shipping, fuel and technology sectors to support the uptake of lower-carbon marine fuels.
The UK Alternative Maritime Fuels Coalition was jointly established by the UK Chamber of Shipping and the Cruise Lines International Association (CLIA), the UK Chamber of Shipping said in an announcement on Tuesday.
It will focus on alternative fuel availability and port infrastructure to support shipping’s transition to net zero.
The coalition will coordinate industry action, contribute to the UK government’s forthcoming consultation on domestic maritime fuel regulation and promote a technology-neutral approach to alternative fuels.
The coalition will meet regularly, with the UK Chamber of Shipping and CLIA acting as joint facilitators.
text:
A new coalition has been launched in the UK to bring together the shipping, fuel and technology sectors to support the uptake of lower-carbon marine fuels.

The UK Alternative Maritime Fuels Coalition was jointly established by the UK Chamber of Shipping and the Cruise Lines International Association (CLIA), the UK Chamber of Shipping said in an announcement on Tuesday.

It will focus on alternative fuel availability and port infrastructure to support shipping’s transition to net zero.

It will also address the policy measures needed to encourage investment in alternative marine fuels and related infrastructure.

Members include IBIA, SEA-LNG, Hydrogen UK, eFuel Alliance, MI - The Global Methanol Alliance and the UK Ammonia Alliance, among others.

The coalition will coordinate industry action, contribute to the UK government’s forthcoming consultation on domestic maritime fuel regulation and promote a technology-neutral approach to alternative fuels.

It will also call for maritime revenues from the UK Emissions Trading Scheme to support shipping decarbonisation, including fuel production, port infrastructure and technology deployment.

The coalition will meet regularly, with the UK Chamber of Shipping and CLIA acting as joint facilitators.

text:
LONDON: India participated in the 22nd Session of the International Maritime Organization’s Intersessional Working Group on Greenhouse Gas Emissions (ISWG-GHG 22), held from 1–4 September 2026, contributing actively to key deliberations concerning the implementation of the IMO Net-Zero Framework and the future pathway for the decarbonisation of international shipping.

The Indian delegation was led by Shri Satish Devdas Kamath, Principal Officer, MMD Kandla, and included Shri C.P.K. Kashyap and Shri Mudit Mehrotra, representing India’s maritime interests during the discussions.

The session brought together IMO Member States to deliberate on critical issues related to the implementation of the IMO’s climate ambitions and the transition of international shipping towards lower and zero greenhouse gas emissions.

During the deliberations, India presented a balanced and pragmatic approach towards the implementation of the IMO Net-Zero Framework. India emphasised the importance of adopting a phased and practical transition that takes into account technological readiness, the availability and affordability of alternative fuels, infrastructure preparedness and the diverse circumstances of Member States.

India’s key interventions focused on the need for a preparatory phase to assess the readiness and practical feasibility of alternative fuels and emerging technologies before the implementation of major measures. Such a phase would help stakeholders better understand the operational, technological and economic challenges associated with the transition to cleaner fuels.

India also advocated for an experience-building phase before the introduction of significant measures. This approach would enable Member States and the shipping industry to gain practical experience, assess implementation challenges and develop informed solutions based on real-world operational experience.

On the issue of future economic measures, India emphasised that such measures should be evidence-based, practical and equitable, while recognising the varying national circumstances, developmental priorities and capacities of Member States. India underlined the importance of ensuring that the global transition towards low- and zero-emission shipping remains inclusive and does not disproportionately impact developing countries.

The session reflected broad support among Member States for the objectives of the 2023 IMO Greenhouse Gas Strategy. India’s constructive interventions and its call for preparatory and experience-building phases received encouraging support from several Member States.

India’s participation at ISWG-GHG 22 reaffirmed the country’s commitment to contributing actively and constructively to international efforts aimed at reducing greenhouse gas emissions from shipping.

As the global maritime industry moves towards a low-carbon future, India continues to advocate for a transition that is practical, inclusive, technologically feasible and equitable. The country remains committed to working closely with the International Maritime Organization and Member States to develop a balanced pathway for the decarbonisation of international shipping while safeguarding the interests and developmental needs of all nations.

India’s engagement at ISWG-GHG 22 highlights its continued commitment to shaping a sustainable and equitable future for global shipping, ensuring that the transition towards net-zero emissions is guided by practicality, collaboration and shared responsibility.

Ambassador Sheikh Abdullah bin Mohammed bin Saud Al-Thani met IMO Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez

Qatar has acceded to Annex VI of the MARPOL convention, the part of the treaty that sets sulphur and NOx limits for marine fuels and engines and would carry the IMO's Net-Zero Framework if it is adopted.

The country's ambassador to the UK and permanent representative to the IMO, Sheikh Abdullah bin Mohammed bin Saud Al-Thani, deposited the instrument of accession to the 1997 Protocol at a meeting with IMO Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez at the organisation's London headquarters on Friday, the Qatar News Agency reported.

The two discussed the accession's role in supporting international efforts to reduce air pollution from ships and protect the marine environment, as well as wider cooperation between Qatar and the IMO, according to the agency.

They also discussed developments in the Strait of Hormuz and "the importance of ensuring the safety and continuity of maritime navigation and international trade through vital waterways in accordance with the provisions of international law," it said.

Annex VI entered into force in May 2005, and under the convention's terms a state's accession takes effect three months after the instrument is deposited.

Ships flagged in states that are not party to the annex are already subject to its requirements when calling at the ports of states that are, so the practical effect of accession is to bring Qatar's own flag administration and ports formally within the regime.

title: Climate Group's NTU Study Calls for "Fingerprinting" of Green Bunkers to Stop Feedstock Fraud
description:
ISCC may dominate the market, the authors find, with more than 90% of biofuels in the UK ISCC-certified and 7,546 ISCC certificates issued in 2024 against 72 for RSB.
It also calls for a central database logging every transaction so that the same batch of fuel cannot be claimed as green more than once, pointing to the EU's Union Database as the model.
That is one side of a live debate at the IMO, where the US has proposed regional ILUC risk rules in submission ISWG-GHG 21/3/21.
For Singapore, the report recommends expanding the pool of trained sustainability auditors as well as adopting fingerprinting, which the campaign group says would strengthen the country's position as a trusted green maritime hub.
The framework the certification rules are meant to serve has yet to be adopted: the Net-Zero Framework failed to pass at last October's extraordinary session and is due back before the Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC) on November 30, with a resumed adoption session pencilled in for December 4.
text:
Study commissioned by campaign group Pacific Environment, carried out by NTU Singapore's MESD centre

Reviews ISCC, RSB, RenovaBio, California's LCFS, and the US RFS as models for the IMO's certification rules

Recommends chemical testing of fuels and a central database against double-counting

Urges IMO to cap or phase out high-ILUC crop feedstocks; report says MPA reviewed it

The most recent cases of feedstock fraud in biofuel certification involved virgin crop oils being passed off as waste used cooking oil (UCO) and palm oil mill effluent (POME), and were only uncovered when the volumes declared became implausible, according to a study published on Tuesday that argues paper-based checks will not be enough as the IMO writes its own fuel certification rules.

The study was commissioned by Pacific Environment, a US-based climate campaign group, and carried out by the Maritime Energy and Sustainable Development (MESD) centre of excellence at Nanyang Technological University in Singapore, with the port authority MPA reviewing the report before publication, according to its acknowledgements.

It reviews the voluntary ISCC and RSB schemes used under the EU's Renewable Energy Directive and CORSIA, alongside Brazil's RenovaBio, California's Low Carbon Fuel Standard, and the US Renewable Fuel Standard, as blueprints for the sustainable fuel certification schemes (SFCS) the IMO is developing for its Net-Zero Framework.

ISCC may dominate the market, the authors find, with more than 90% of biofuels in the UK ISCC-certified and 7,546 ISCC certificates issued in 2024 against 72 for RSB.

Fingerprinting

To counter feedstock fraud the study recommends chemical testing, or "fingerprinting", to verify what a fuel was made from independently of its paperwork, though it says this is "subject to further methodology development and a cost-benefit analysis", and notes Singapore has already developed such a method using methanol as a case study.

It also calls for a central database logging every transaction so that the same batch of fuel cannot be claimed as green more than once, pointing to the EU's Union Database as the model.

"As shipping scales up the use of these fuels, we need certification systems that are robust enough to guard against fraud and unsustainable production, while also being practical and workable across complex international supply chains," said Pacific Environment's Singapore climate specialist Lim Jie Ying in an emailed press release.

Land Use

The study finds the biggest gap between the schemes is the treatment of indirect land-use change (ILUC), the emissions caused when fuel crops displace food production and drive deforestation elsewhere, which CORSIA and the two US schemes count but the EU schemes do not.

The study's authors recommend a hybrid approach, using quantitative ILUC values to penalise the carbon intensity of crop-based biofuels while still allowing their use, with usage caps or an eventual phase-out for high-risk feedstocks.

That is one side of a live debate at the IMO, where the US has proposed regional ILUC risk rules in submission ISWG-GHG 21/3/21.

"Strengthening the traceability of sustainable fuels through continued research and innovation will be critical in supporting the maritime energy transition," said the study's lead researcher, Dr Yeoh Keat Ping, research lead at MESD.

For Singapore, the report recommends expanding the pool of trained sustainability auditors as well as adopting fingerprinting, which the campaign group says would strengthen the country's position as a trusted green maritime hub.

The framework the certification rules are meant to serve has yet to be adopted: the Net-Zero Framework failed to pass at last October's extraordinary session and is due back before the Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC) on November 30, with a resumed adoption session pencilled in for December 4.

The Polish energy company ORLEN and the Port of Gdynia Authority have signed an agreement to explore the use of LNG and bioLNG as marine vessel fuels.

ORLEN’s cooperation with the Port of Gdynia will cover an assessment of market demand, the potential for LNG and bioLNG bunkering, as well as the necessary infrastructure, operational conditions and regulatory requirements needed to develop such services. One of the key areas under review will be the feasibility of waterside bunkering, including ship-to-ship operations, where fuel is transferred directly from a bunker vessel to a ship in port.

Robert Soszyński, Vice President of the ORLEN Management Board, Operations, say that ‘Our expanded cooperation with the Port of Gdynia marks an important step in developing the LNG and bioLNG market in the Tricity area and forms part of a wider transformation of ORLEN’s fuel portfolio through 2035. Under the ORLEN Group’s strategy, gas, including LNG, will play a strategic role as a transitional fuel supporting energy security and the decarbonization of transport. Our ambition is to build competitive strengths across the entire value chain – from supply and logistics through to end use. In parallel, we are developing capabilities in renewable fuels, including bioLNG, which could become one of the key pathways to lower emissions in heavy-duty road and maritime transport over the coming years. We want ORLEN to be more than a fuel supplier to ports. We aim to be a partner in their transition, making a genuine contribution to the development of infrastructure and market conditions needed for alternative marine fuels to grow in Poland and the wider region.’

Piotr Gorzeński, CEO of the Port of Gdynia Authority, says that ‘Energy transition in the shipping industry is already under way. Shipowners are looking for solutions that could reduce emissions, while ports need to be ready to accommodate vessels using a range of fuels and technologies. We want the Port of Gdynia to be prepared for what the future may bring, because no one can say with certainty which solutions will matter most 10 or 20 years from now. This is why we’re developing the port to respond to the changing needs of vessels and support reductions in emissions from maritime transport. Our cooperation with ORLEN on LNG and bioLNG bunkering is one of the steps in that direction.’

text:
IBIA's representative to the IMO, Dr Edmund Hughes. Image Credit: IBIA

Multiplier "could potentially replace financial rewards and so the need for revenues to provide them", says IBIA's Dr Edmund Hughes

Without a fund, cash rewards for zero and near-zero fuels "would not be possible", but a non-fiscal route may work

Several states reviewing positions and may be moderating "red lines" after ISWG-GHG 22

Hughes moderates the regulatory panel at the IBIA Annual Convention in New York, November 10-12

IBIA's representative to the IMO, Dr Edmund Hughes, says China's multiplier proposal for zero and near-zero fuels and technologies could be a way round the deadlock over an IMO fund under the Net-Zero Framework (NZF), rewarding green fuels without needing revenues to pay for it.

"Such a multiplier, if designed correctly, could potentially replace financial rewards and so the need for revenues to provide them," he told Ship & Bunker following last week's ISWG-GHG 22.

The fund has proven a key sticking point for the proposed framework, with the US in particular one of its most outspoken critics, criticism that many feel ultimately led to adoption of the NZF being derailed at an extraordinary session last October.

The US delegation reiterated at ISWG-GHG 22 that an IMO-administered fund remains a red line.

China's proposal would apply the multiplier "where funding for monetary rewards is constrained" and have it "operate effectively in conjunction with the use of Surplus Units."

Hughes said it had received support from several member states at the meeting, but was clear about what losing the fund would mean for cash rewards.

"Without provisions for raising and a depositary for receiving revenues from a global measure it would mean financial rewards for the use of ZNZs would not be possible," he said.

"However, alternative approaches for incentivising uptake of ZNZs through widening the scope and use of Surplus Units and the application of a 'multiplier' might provide a non-fiscal solution if linked to other schemes such as Japan's proposal for 'direct voluntary contributions'."

Japan's contributions concept could also be integrated with other schemes to provide funds for the just and equitable transition that is a core principle of the 2023 IMO GHG strategy, he added.

That is a shift in emphasis from the position IBIA and ICS took in their joint submission calling for significant rewards paid from the framework's fund.

Hughes said industry bodies, ICS and IBIA among them, had backed adoption of the framework primarily to secure global regulation of shipping's GHG emissions and "to reduce the risk of proliferation of national/regional measures such as seen under the European Union".

Red Lines

On the week itself, he said "limited progress" had been made, as it was the first time member states had met to consider the proposals to amend the draft framework circulated since Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC) 84 in May, from Brazil, Liberia, Tuvalu, and Japan, and one submitted jointly by Australia, Canada, South Africa, and the UK.

"Despite the remaining divergent views it is evident that following consideration several Member States are reviewing their position and may be moderating their 'red lines' on several of the key policy issues," he said.

A gentler Global Fuel Intensity (GFI) reduction trajectory and greater flexibility in the supply and use of surplus units had been identified by many member states, he said, but they remained divided on the payment by ships for remedial units when unable to comply, and on the establishment of an IMO GHG fund.

Some new proposals had received support, including the idea of a "facility" for managing and disbursing revenues through established institutions rather than the IMO, notably from the US.

"As the Chair of the meeting observed the Group's general view was that the name of the mechanism matters less than its 'nature, purpose and functions' which all remain open for further definition and including how would IMO retain oversight," he said.

The working group closed on Friday with its chair reporting a willingness to present text to MEPC in November, and a UCL readout counting 38 states speaking for a central fund and 17 against.

The topic will be discussed further at the IBIA Annual Convention in New York on November 10-12, where Hughes, who headed the IMO's air pollution and energy efficiency work from 2013 to 2020 and has represented the bunker industry body at the organisation since 2023, moderates the regulatory and policy panel, Navigating a Changing Framework.

text:
Dutch biofuel company Sunoil Biodiesel has received regulatory clearance to supply its sustainable fuel products in Belgium, opening another European market for the company, biofuels international reported.

With the approval, Belgium has joined the growing number of European countries where Sunoil can sell its biodiesel made from waste materials.

The company said expansion into a new country requires systems that can track products properly, meet sustainability standards and comply with local rules at every stage of the supply chain. Sunoil said these measures provide a strong base for its continued expansion across Europe.

The approval comes as the company increases its operations and expands the use of its biodiesel in transport. The fuel is produced in the Netherlands and supplied through a partnership with BFT Tanker Logistics.

Birjo II is now transporting biofuel using 100% renewable fuel, providing an example of how Sunoil’s biodiesel can be used in transport to reduce emissions.

Sunoil produces biodiesel from certified waste oils and fats at its facilities in Emmen and Kampen. The company also operates a trading business in Amsterdam.

Its biodiesel is used as an alternative to fossil-based diesel or mixed with fossil diesel for use in road transport, shipping and the energy sector.
